questions.question: A 45-year-old patient with a history of schizophrenia, admitted 3 days ago for acute psychosis, has been calm since admission on IV haloperidol. This morning he was found anxious, agitated and in respiratory distress, with tachypnoea and significant accessory muscle use. Blood pressure is 150/100 mmHg, heart rate 130/min, temperature 36.5°C, SaO2 100% on room air. Head and neck exam is unremarkable except for a dry tongue; lungs are clear but with accessory muscle use; cardiac sounds are fast but regular without murmur; abdomen is soft, non-tender and non-distended; extremities are normal. He is confused and agitated, localises painful stimuli, opens his eyes spontaneously and replies with words only, mostly due to dyspnoea; muscle tone is not increased. Among the following, which is the most useful test in making a diagnosis at this time?
options: A chest CT with pulmonary embolism protocol
questions.explanation: An acutely dyspnoeic, tachypnoeic patient with a sudden change in mental status needs urgent assessment of oxygenation, ventilation and acid-base status. An arterial blood gas is the fastest way to identify hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, or a metabolic derangement (e.g. neuroleptic malignant syndrome, serotonin-related toxicity, or an unrelated cause such as pulmonary embolism) and guides immediate management. A chest x-ray, CT-PA, ECG or echocardiogram may follow depending on the ABG result, but none gives the same immediate physiological picture.

questions.question: The following statement regarding gastric lavage is correct EXCEPT:
options: It may cause increased absorption of some poisons
It is contraindicated with caustic ingestions
It should not be performed before intubation of a patient in coma
It is most useful in mildly symptomatic intoxications
questions.explanation: Gastric lavage is now rarely used and, when considered, is reserved for potentially life-threatening ingestions presenting within about an hour — not mild, self-limiting intoxications, where the risks (aspiration, mucosal injury, and increased systemic absorption of some poisons by propelling them into the small bowel) outweigh any benefit. It is contraindicated after caustic ingestion, and should not be attempted in a comatose patient before the airway is protected. 'Most useful in mildly symptomatic intoxications' is therefore the false statement — the opposite is closer to the truth.

questions.question: A university student called the ambulance after finding his roommate unconscious in the bedroom. He was the last person to see him well the previous night, about 5 hours before the ambulance call. The victim has a history of bipolar disorder and an empty pill bottle of lithium was found near his bed. In the Emergency Department the patient was intubated, given IV fluids and started on a noradrenaline infusion. He was sedated with propofol 100 mg/hr. His blood pressure was 110/65 mmHg, heart rate 100 beats per minute and temperature 36°C. SaO2 was 100% on FiO2 50% and the respiratory rate 12 breaths per minute as per ventilator. The most appropriate action now is:
options: Insert nasogastric tube and perform gastric lavage
Administer 100 g of activated charcoal via nasogastric tube
Administer sodium bicarbonate 100 ml bolus intravenously
questions.explanation: None of the listed interventions is appropriate here. Gastric lavage is only useful within a short window after ingestion, and oral activated charcoal does not adsorb lithium ions at all. Sodium bicarbonate has no effect on lithium excretion. Charcoal haemoperfusion is not the standard extracorporeal technique for lithium — haemodialysis is, since lithium is one of the most readily dialysable toxins — but haemodialysis was not offered as an option, making 'none of the above' correct.

questions.question: A 67-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department in a comatose state. He was found by the cleaning lady in the morning, lying on the living room floor. He was intubated on arrival to the ED, given IV fluids and started on noradrenaline infusion. The paramedics found empty pill bottles of amitriptyline, verapamil, aspirin, zolpidem and quetiapine. On exam, blood pressure is 90/40 mmHg, heart rate 120/min, temperature is 35°C and SaO2 is 92% on 100% FiO2. The lung exam revealed diffuse bilateral crackles, cardiac exam showed irregular rate and rhythm without a murmur, abdomen was mildly distended, soft, and tympanic to percussion. Extremities were cold with mild ankle edema but no cyanosis. There was no urine in the urinary catheter collecting bag, inserted 1 hour previously. All is true at this time EXCEPT:
options: He will need admission to ICU
Poison control center needs to be called as soon as possible
questions.explanation: This patient has ingested a combination of a tricyclic antidepressant, a calcium-channel blocker, aspirin, zolpidem and quetiapine and is now in shock — he clearly needs ICU admission, and the poison control centre should be involved early given the polypharmacy. Gastric lavage is not indicated this long after a mixed, already-symptomatic ingestion, and paracetamol levels should always be checked in a deliberate overdose to exclude co-ingestion. Hemodialysis is not indicated on this information alone — none of the ingested agents is reliably removed by haemodialysis at this stage, and dialysis is not routine treatment for shock in a mixed cardiotoxic overdose — making it the exception (false) statement.

questions.question: A 45-year-old patient with schizophrenia, previously calm for 3 days on IV haloperidol, developed acute anxiety, agitation and respiratory distress with tachypnoea and significant accessory muscle use (blood pressure 150/100 mmHg, heart rate 130/min). Further testing reveals an arterial blood gas: pH 7.13, pCO2 20 mmHg, pO2 100 mmHg, HCO3- 8 mEq/L. Point-of-care sodium is 140 mEq/L, chloride 98 mEq/L, glucose 125 mg/dL, and potassium 4 mEq/L. The ECG showed sinus tachycardia with non-specific ST and T changes in the precordial leads, and the chest x-ray was normal. At this point the LEAST appropriate action is:
options: Check for serum and urine ketones
questions.explanation: This picture — tachypnoea with a mixed, high anion-gap metabolic acidosis (anion gap ≈34) and normal chest imaging — should prompt a search for a toxic or metabolic cause: ketones, salicylate, osmolar gap (toxic alcohols) and lactate are all standard, useful parts of this work-up. He has only been receiving therapeutic IV haloperidol, which does not itself cause a high anion-gap metabolic acidosis, so measuring a serum haloperidol level would not clarify the diagnosis and is the least appropriate test here.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department by a tourist office operator. She came back to her hotel from a bar complaining of dyspnoea and visual trouble. On physical examination, her speech was slightly slurred, she had a GCS of 14 (E4V4M6) as she was not oriented in either time or place. Her breath smelled of alcohol. Her blood pressure was 140/75 mmHg, heart rate 120 beats per minute, respiratory rate 45 breaths per minute, temperature 36°C and SpO2 100% on room air. Apart from the use of accessory muscles and tachypnoea, the physical exam was unremarkable. The fingerstick glucose was 80 mg/dL (4.4 mmol/L). According to the tour group operator she had no significant past medical history and took no medications. The next most appropriate action now is to:
options: Administer a bolus of 500 ml normal saline IV
Perform an arterial blood gas analysis
Admit and observe in a medical ward
questions.explanation: Acute alcohol intoxication is a clinically harmful condition that usually follows the ingestion of a large amount of alcohol. Criteria include recent alcohol ingestion, clinically significant maladaptive behavioural or psychological changes developing during or shortly after ingestion, and signs such as slurred speech, incoordination, unsteady gait, nystagmus, impaired attention or memory, or stupor/coma that are not due to a general medical condition and cannot be explained by another mental disorder. Multiple conditions can mimic acute alcohol intoxication — other substance intoxication, metabolic derangement, neurological causes including seizure and trauma, infection, hypotension, hypo- or hyperthermia, hypo- or hyperthyroidism, dehydration, hypoxia and respiratory depression — and should be excluded. A blood gas analysis is a quick way to check for metabolic and hydro-electrolytic derangement, which this patient's marked tachypnoea makes essential before assuming simple intoxication.

questions.question: A 23-year-old woman without significant past medical history is transferred intubated from the Emergency Department to the ICU. She was initially brought from her home after ingesting an unknown amount of amitriptyline tablets. In the Emergency Department she was agitated and suffered convulsions that were treated with diazepam 10 mg IV; her blood pressure was 87/45 mmHg and the heart rate was 123 beats per minute. The patient was then intubated and 80 grams of charcoal were given via nasogastric tube after intubation. In the ICU she was sedated with propofol 300 mg/hr and started on a noradrenaline infusion. Pupils were 5 mm wide, equal in size and reactive to light. Lungs were clear to auscultation. Abdominal and extremities exam was unremarkable. Heart sounds were irregular and, on the ECG monitor, there were polymorphic premature ventricular complexes. An arterial blood gas was performed on FiO2 45% and reported the following values: pH 7.45, pCO2 45 mmHg (6 kPa), pO2 108 mmHg (14.4 kPa), HCO3- 23 mmol/L. A 12-lead ECG showed a QRS duration of 0.17 seconds on limb leads. Which of the following is most appropriate at this time?
questions.explanation: Sodium bicarbonate is indicated for the treatment of dysrhythmias or hypotension associated with TCA overdose, and may be considered for QRS prolongation (>100 ms) associated with TCA overdose. Treatment of dysrhythmias or hypotension should include alkalinisation to a serum pH of 7.45–7.55. Sodium-channel blocking medications — class Ia (procainamide), Ib (lidocaine) and Ic (flecainide) antiarrhythmics — as well as beta-blockers and amiodarone should be avoided, as they may worsen hypotension and conduction abnormalities.

questions.question: A 36-year-old hairdresser was found in her home severely agitated and confused. She was brought to the Emergency Department where she was then intubated because of the need for sedation and subsequent loss of airway reflexes. Suction via the endotracheal tube produced copious clear secretions. She was hypotensive, was given 1 L of NaCl 0.9% and started on a noradrenaline drip to keep a systolic blood pressure above 90 mmHg. The patient's heart rate was 40 beats per minute, respiratory rate was set at 18 breaths per minute and temperature was 37.8°C. Pupils were 1 mm wide and sluggish. Lung examination revealed diffuse crackles and wheezing bilaterally. Cardiac sounds were regular and slow. The abdomen was soft, moderately distended with increased bowel sounds. Extremities were warm without cyanosis. She was moving all four extremities equally before intubation. According to her friend, she does not take any medications and has no chronic illnesses, but he was suspicious when he found a powder-like substance covering the victim's kitchen table. The patient had an unremarkable urgent brain CT on admission. The ECG showed sinus bradycardia without ischemic changes. The arterial blood gas analysis reported: pH 7.35, pCO2 35 mmHg (4.6 kPa), pO2 80 mmHg (10.6 kPa), HCO3- 19 mEq/L and lactate 4 mmol/L; gap is 8. The most likely cause for the patient's condition is:
questions.explanation: The powder-like substance on the kitchen table points to either a substance overdose or insecticide toxicity, and the clinical picture — bradycardia, miosis and bronchorrhea — makes insecticide/organophosphate toxicity most likely. Heroin overdose is unlikely given the picture, and cocaine intoxication typically produces tachycardia, hypertension and increased sympathetic tone rather than bradycardia and copious secretions. Organophosphates inhibit cholinesterase, causing acetylcholine accumulation at synapses and overstimulation of both central and peripheral nervous systems. Peripheral effects occur at muscarinic receptors (excessive salivation, miosis, bronchorrhea, diarrhoea) and nicotinic receptors (increased or decreased muscle power, fasciculations). The most frequent signs are miosis, vomiting, hypersalivation, respiratory distress, abdominal pain, depressed consciousness and muscle fasciculations — all present here.

questions.question: Three patients are brought to the Emergency Department complaining of nausea, dizziness and headache after having had lunch together. There is no history of chronic diseases. On exam they are fully alert and communicating without focal deficits. Their lips and tongues have a bluish discoloration. They show no respiratory distress. The lungs are clear and cardiac exam is normal except for a mild tachycardia. Abdominal exam is normal except for mild discomfort on palpation of the epigastrium. Extremities are cyanotic but not cold. Pulse oximetry shows a saturation of 97%. They are not hypotensive and their temperature measurements are between 36°C and 37°C. Which from the following will be most helpful in making a diagnosis?
options: An arterial blood gas with cooximetry
questions.explanation: Methemoglobinemia is an unusual and potentially fatal condition in which haemoglobin is oxidised to methemoglobin and loses its ability to bind and transport oxygen — typically from ingestion or inhalation of an oxidising agent. Signs (methemoglobin above 10%) include shortness of breath, cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen despite a near-normal pulse oximetry reading, mental status change, headache, fatigue and dizziness; levels above 50% may cause seizures, coma and death. Elevated methemoglobin occurs when the red cell's defences against oxidative stress are overwhelmed and the ferrous iron (Fe2+) of haemoglobin is oxidised to the ferric state (Fe3+), reducing oxygen delivery to tissues. Arterial blood with elevated methemoglobin has a characteristic chocolate-brown colour compared with normal bright-red oxygenated blood. Standard pulse oximetry cannot distinguish this, so an arterial blood gas with co-oximetry should be obtained — a shared exposure (lunch together) with cyanosis and a normal SpO2 is a classic trigger for this diagnosis.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man with a history of schizophrenia was found unconscious in the lobby of his apartment. A neighbour called for help and an ambulance brought the patient to the Emergency Room. No other medical history is available. On examination, blood pressure was 140/80 mmHg, heart rate 120 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and temperature was 36°C. The patient was somnolent with a GCS of 9 (E2V2M5). Pupils were 5 mm wide, equal bilateral and reactive. He flexed the upper extremities equally to pain. There was no nuchal rigidity and muscle tone was normal. Breathing occurred without distress, the lungs were clear on auscultation and the cardiac exam was unremarkable except for tachycardia. The patient was also sweating profusely, mainly on the face. Which of the following actions is the most appropriate at this time?
options: Perform finger stick for glucose measurement
Administer a 500 ml normal saline bolus
Insert a nasogastric tube and perform gastric lavage
questions.explanation: The unconscious patient's airway, breathing and circulation should be quickly assessed and concurrently treated. Ensuring patency of the airway is an overriding initial priority to allow oxygenation and ventilation, and the cervical spine should be immobilised if injury is possible. A rapid initial survey should follow, looking for injury or other notable findings of the head, neck, chest, abdomen and extremities. IV access should be established quickly, and bedside blood glucose testing should be performed in all unconscious patients — diaphoresis and tachycardia here are classic hypoglycaemia signs. If glucose is <70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L), 50 ml of 50% dextrose should be given IV, with thiamine 100 mg IV in patients at risk of nutritional deficiency. If opioid toxicity is suspected (history of illicit drug use, apnoea or bradypnea, small pupils), naloxone 0.4–2 mg IV should be given and repeated as needed, up to 4 mg; physostigmine may be given for anticholinergic toxicity in selected patients. Reference: Stevens R, Cadena R, Pineda J. Emergency Neurological Life Support: Approach to the Patient with Coma, Neurocritical Care 2015.

questions.question: Which of the following is correct regarding intoxications?
options: Accidental poisoning is the most common mode of poisoning in adults
Patient's history is the most reliable account of the type and amount of poisons taken
Most patients with drug induced coma will improve after the first 12 hours of presentation
Lateralizing neurological findings are common in the poisoned patient
In every patient suspected of poisoning a thorough history and physical examination should take place before any action is taken
questions.explanation: Among adults, the most common exposures are due to intentional ingestion of analgesics, sedatives, antipsychotics and antidepressants — not accidental poisoning. Patients with acute drug poisoning are relatively common in hospitals, usually require relatively simple care and have a good short-term outcome; a typical symptom is decreasing consciousness, going from sedation to coma, and most improve within the first 12 hours of presentation. History is often difficult to elicit and unreliable rather than the most trustworthy source, lateralising neurological findings are uncommon in poisoning (and should raise suspicion of a structural cause), and emergency stabilisation should not be delayed for a complete history and exam when the patient is unstable.

questions.question: After being found unconscious in a park, a 20-year-old man was brought to the hospital with a low level of consciousness. Medical history is not available. Paramedics report no evidence of external injury. The physical examination showed a man with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 3 and small, symmetrical, equal pupils, with sluggish reaction to light. Additionally, he showed decreased muscle tone and hyporeflexia, but no nuchal rigidity. Respiratory rate was 6 breaths per minute, blood pressure 90/50 mmHg, heart rate 55 beats per minute and temperature 36°C. What is the best therapeutic option in this case?
options: Insertion of a nasogastric tube and gastric lavage
Insertion of a nasogastric tube and administration of activated charcoal
questions.explanation: This patient most probably has an opioid intoxication. Respiratory depression is the most consistent and important clinical sign of opioid toxicity — a respiratory rate under 12/min in a patient who is not simply asleep is highly suggestive of acute opioid intoxication. Constricted pupils (miosis) or poor arousability in a slow-breathing patient further suggest opioid toxicity, although miosis alone is nonspecific (anticonvulsants, antipsychotics, alcohol and benzodiazepines can also cause it, usually without respiratory depression). The correct antidote here is naloxone IV.

questions.question: A 16-year-old girl was found unconscious in her room an hour after having argued with her parents. She had a history of anxiety and depression and takes alprazolam and paroxetine regularly. There were no other known medical problems. In the Emergency Department she had a Glasgow Coma Score of 7 (E1V2M4). Pupils were 4 mm wide, equal and reactive bilaterally to light. There was no nuchal rigidity but muscle tone was decreased. Breathing was shallow and produced abnormal breathing sounds. Blood pressure was 80/40 mmHg, heart rate 110 beats per minute, respiratory rate 40 breaths per minute and temperature 36°C. SpO2 was 91% with a non-rebreathing oxygen mask at 15 L/min. Appropriate immediate actions at this time are:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Administer a bolus of 500 ml of normal saline

statements.label: D
statements.text: Administer activated charcoal via nasogastric tube

questions.explanation: Disorders of consciousness such as coma are potentially life-threatening and warrant a rapid, structured approach: an ABC approach ensuring first adequacy of airway, then breathing and circulatory function, is the initial priority — this hypotensive, hypoxic, poorly protected patient needs both fluid resuscitation and preparation for intubation. Flumazenil is not given routinely in benzodiazepine overdose because of seizure risk, particularly with mixed or unclear ingestions. A single oral dose of activated charcoal should not be given routinely after acute poisoning; it may help if given within 1 hour of ingestion of an adsorbable agent, but there is no evidence for benefit beyond that window, and airway protection must be considered first — not appropriate as an immediate action in a patient with GCS 7 and an unprotected airway.

questions.question: For the following substances there is a specific antidote:
questions.explanation: Methanol toxicity is treated with fomepizole (or ethanol) as an alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitor. Iron overdose has a specific antidote, the chelator deferoxamine. Digoxin toxicity has a specific antidote, digoxin-specific antibody fragments (DigiFab/Digibind). Haloperidol overdose has no specific antidote; management is supportive.

questions.question: A 70-year-old retired school teacher is brought to the Emergency Department confused and agitated. His wife called an ambulance when she found him in the garden around 11 AM; he had been spraying plants since 8 AM. On arrival, his blood pressure was 180/100 mmHg, heart rate 45 beats per minute, respiratory rate 38 breaths per minute and temperature was 38°C. SpO2 was 94% on a non-rebreathing oxygen mask at 15 L/min. He was confused, agitated and moved all 4 extremities equally. Pupils were 2 mm wide and sluggishly reactive to light. Lung examination revealed coarse crackles and wheezing in all lung fields. Cardiac exam revealed sinus bradycardia. Abdominal exam revealed increased bowel sounds. Extremities were warm without cyanosis. His wife provided a history of hypertension treated with lisinopril and type II diabetes treated with glibenclamide. The following statements are true/false:

statements.label: A
statements.text: The most likely etiology for the patient's condition is opiate overdose

statements.label: B
statements.text: The patient's clothes should be removed

statements.label: C
statements.text: A fingerstick for glucose should be performed

questions.explanation: Organophosphate compounds are used as commercial insecticides, and organophosphate poisoning is still a frequent reason for ICU admission — this patient's miosis, bradycardia, bronchorrhea/wheeze and increased bowel sounds (muscarinic effects, remembered as SLUDGE: salivation, lacrimation, urination, diaphoresis, GI upset, emesis) fit organophosphate exposure during spraying, not opiate overdose, which would not explain the hypertension or bronchorrhea. General measures include terminating exposure by removing all soiled clothing and washing the skin with soap and water; securing the airway with intubation if needed for laryngospasm, bronchospasm, bronchorrhea or seizures; and continuous cardiac monitoring with a 12-lead ECG, since QT prolongation and Torsades de Pointes can occur and should be treated in the standard manner. A glibenclamide-treated diabetic who has been agitated and unwell for hours also warrants a glucose check regardless of the toxicological picture.

questions.question: A 66-year-old man is brought unconscious to the Emergency Department. His wife called an ambulance when she found him on the bathroom floor. On arrival, he was endotracheally intubated and had a GCS score of 4 (E1V1M2). His wife reported that he had had a myocardial infarction with percutaneous coronary angioplasty and multiple stent placement 3 years ago, and had been severely depressed for about a year. His usual medication included aspirin 100 mg daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, carvedilol 25 mg bid and sertraline 10 mg daily. According to his wife, he was well until 30 minutes before she found him; there was no history of headache, behavioural change or fever, and she did not see any empty pill containers. The patient was given etomidate 20 mg, midazolam 5 mg and cisatracurium 10 mg IV for intubation and airway protection, and is now on a propofol infusion at 100 mg/hr. Blood pressure was 180/80 mmHg, heart rate 55 beats per minute and temperature 36°C; respiratory rate was set at 14 breaths per minute. There was no nuchal rigidity before intubation. The left pupil was 3 mm wide and reacting to light; the right pupil was 6 mm wide and non-reactive. Muscle tone was absent. The lungs were clear on auscultation, and cardiac exam revealed a regular, bradycardic rhythm without murmurs. The abdominal exam was unremarkable; there was mild bilateral ankle edema. Appropriate actions to do next are:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Perform a brain CT as soon as possible

statements.label: B
statements.text: Wait until the medications wear off and then re-examine the patient

statements.label: C
statements.text: Administer intravenous agents to lower the blood pressure

statements.label: D
statements.text: Perform a qualitative urine toxicology screen

questions.explanation: A focal neurological finding — here a fixed, dilated, non-reactive right pupil against a normal, reactive left pupil — in a patient found suddenly unconscious raises concern for a structural intracranial process (e.g. haemorrhage with early uncal herniation) rather than a purely toxic-metabolic cause, even in a patient with a psychiatric history and sedative drugs on board. This mandates an urgent brain CT rather than simply waiting for medications to wear off. Empirically lowering blood pressure is not appropriate before the cause of coma is known, since hypertension may be a compensatory (Cushing) response to raised intracranial pressure. A urine toxicology screen is unlikely to change immediate management and should not delay definitive imaging.

questions.question: A 21-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department by her husband. She is drowsy with a GCS of 11 (E3V3M5). Her husband states he found an empty bottle of alprazolam, but he is not sure how much was in it, and cannot say when the pills were taken. Three hours earlier they had an argument, he left the house, and when he came back he found her drowsy. On further exam, blood pressure is 135/75 mmHg, heart rate 90 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute and temperature 36°C. SaO2 is 99% on room air. There is no respiratory distress and no abnormal breath sounds. Lungs are clear, cardiac and abdominal examinations are unremarkable. Extremities have decreased tone but no cyanosis. Which are correct actions at this time?

statements.label: A
statements.text: The patient should be admitted to the ICU for further care

statements.label: B
statements.text: She should be put on a flumazenil infusion

statements.label: D
statements.text: A gastric lavage should be performed

questions.explanation: Alprazolam is a short-acting benzodiazepine used for anxiety disorders. It is considered more toxic in overdose than other benzodiazepines, with rapid oral absorption, peak levels at 1–2 hours, high protein binding, hepatic metabolism and an elimination half-life of 12–15 hours. Overdose causes drowsiness, ataxia and slurred speech; conscious state can steadily decrease, putting the patient at risk of airway obstruction, hypoxia and aspiration, and very large ingestions can rarely cause cardiovascular compromise, bradycardia, hypotension and hypothermia — none of which is present here. As in most benzodiazepine overdoses with no cardiovascular compromise, supportive care (usually overnight observation with psychiatric review once conscious state improves) is sufficient; ICU admission, a flumazenil infusion (seizure risk, and not indicated without airway compromise) and gastric lavage (outside the window and not indicated in a haemodynamically stable, non-comatose patient) are not appropriate. Co-ingestion should always be considered in a deliberate overdose, including agents like paracetamol, so a paracetamol level should be checked.

questions.question: A university student called the ambulance after finding his roommate unconscious in the bedroom. He was the last person to see him well about 5 hours before the ambulance call. The victim has a history of bipolar disorder and an empty pill bottle of lithium was found near his bed. In the Emergency Department, the patient was intubated, given IV fluids and started on a noradrenaline infusion due to fluid-unresponsive hypotension. He was sedated with propofol 100 mg/hr. His blood pressure was 110/47 mmHg, heart rate 100 beats per minute and temperature 36°C. SpO2 was 98% on FiO2 35% and the respiratory rate 12 breaths per minute as per ventilator. The most appropriate action now is:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Insert nasogastric tube and perform gastric lavage

statements.label: B
statements.text: Administer 100 g of activated charcoal via nasogastric tube

statements.label: C
statements.text: Administer sodium bicarbonate 100 ml bolus intravenously

questions.explanation: Lithium has been used as the gold standard treatment for major depressive and bipolar disorders for decades; because of its narrow therapeutic index, lithium toxicity is a common clinical problem. The general approach to a lithium-intoxicated patient resembles other poisonings — airway management, especially with altered mental status, and gastric lavage when the patient presents shortly after intoxication — which is not the case 5 hours out here. Oral activated charcoal has no effect, as it cannot bind lithium ions, and bicarbonate has no effect on lithium excretion. Lithium is one of the most readily dialysable toxins; extracorporeal removal is the mainstay once significantly toxic, and charcoal haemoperfusion — where blood is perfused through a filter of activated carbon or another microporous material, a technique developed since the 1940s — remains available for this purpose even though it is now used only infrequently.

questions.question: A 67-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department in a coma state. He was found by the cleaning lady in the morning, lying on the living room floor. He was intubated on arrival to the ED, given IV fluids and started on a noradrenaline infusion. The paramedics found empty pill bottles of amitriptyline, verapamil, aspirin, zolpidem and quetiapine. On exam, blood pressure was 90/40 mmHg, heart rate 120 beats per minute, temperature was 35°C and SaO2 92% on 100% FiO2. The lung exam revealed diffuse bilateral crackles, the cardiac exam showed an irregular rate and rhythm without a murmur, abdomen was mildly distended, soft, and tympanic to percussion. Extremities were cold with mild ankle edema but no cyanosis. There was no urine in the urinary catheter collecting bag, inserted 1 hour previously. Which of the following are true at this time?

statements.label: A
statements.text: The poison control center needs to be called as soon as possible

questions.explanation: Given the polypharmacy overdose (tricyclic antidepressant, calcium-channel blocker, aspirin, zolpidem, quetiapine) and current shock, the poison control centre should be involved as soon as possible, and paracetamol levels should always be checked in a deliberate mixed overdose to exclude co-ingestion. Gastric lavage is not indicated this long after ingestion in an already-symptomatic patient. Hemodialysis is not indicated on this information alone — none of the ingested agents is reliably removed by haemodialysis at this stage, and it is not routine treatment for shock in mixed cardiotoxic overdose.

questions.question: A 56-year-old man is found unconscious at home and brought to the Emergency Department. He was started on oxygen 15 L/min via non-rebreathing mask; SpO2 was 90%, blood pressure 110/65 mmHg, heart rate 120/min, respiratory rate 40/min, temperature 36°C, breathing deep and laboured. Pupils were 4 mm, equal and reactive. He moaned to pain and flexed both upper extremities but did not open his eyes. He has a history of hypertension treated with amlodipine and has been drinking excess alcohol for about a year, since his wife died. He lives alone; family last spoke to him by phone the previous night around 10 PM and he sounded fine. No empty pill bottles were found, but there were 3 empty beer bottles nearby. An arterial blood gas just before intubation showed: pH 7.05, pCO2 30 mmHg, pO2 65 mmHg, HCO3- 10 mEq/L. You decide to intubate the patient. When intubating this patient extra caution is required because:

statements.label: B
statements.text: There is increased risk for hypotension

statements.label: C
statements.text: The time of last meal is not known

questions.explanation: This patient has a severe, decompensated metabolic acidosis (pH 7.05, HCO3- 10) with respiratory compensation (tachypnoea, low pCO2). Induction agents and positive-pressure ventilation can precipitate hypotension and cardiovascular collapse in severely acidotic patients, and any drop in minute ventilation during intubation removes the respiratory compensation, worsening the acidaemia. His unknown last-meal time raises aspiration risk, and his tachycardia reflects physiological compensation that can be blunted by induction agents — all of these make airway management higher-risk and warrant extra caution and preparation.

questions.question: A 56-year-old man was found unconscious at home with deep, laboured breathing (SpO2 90% on a non-rebreathing mask, moaning and flexing to pain only, not opening his eyes) and a history of alcohol use since his wife's death. An arterial blood gas prior to intubation showed pH 7.05, pCO2 30 mmHg, pO2 65 mmHg, HCO3- 10 mEq/L, consistent with a severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. He is now intubated without complications and placed on mechanical ventilation. Which of the following need to be done regarding work-up of this patient?
questions.explanation: All of the above work-up investigations are part of the standard laboratory work-up required to investigate an unconscious patient with an unexplained severe metabolic acidosis: the anion gap and osmolar gap help identify a toxic-alcohol ingestion (e.g. ethylene glycol, methanol), lactate distinguishes a lactic acidosis, and paracetamol levels should be checked in any patient with a possible deliberate ingestion.

questions.question: A 56-year-old man was intubated for coma with a severe metabolic acidosis of unclear cause (history of alcohol use since his wife's death; no pill bottles found, only empty beer bottles). New arterial blood gases are: pH 7.1, pCO2 25 mmHg, pO2 85 mmHg, HCO3- 10 mEq/L, on FiO2 50%. Chemistry panel: Na+ 140 mEq/L, K+ 3.5–4 mEq/L, Cl- 100 mEq/L, glucose 5 mmol/L (90 mg/dL), urea 6 mmol/L, creatinine 2.5 mg/dL (221 µmol/L). Serum osmolality is 330 mOsm/kg. Lactate is 2 mmol/L. In view of the above laboratory findings, the following will be helpful in the diagnosis:
questions.explanation: A raised anion gap with a raised osmolar gap and only mildly elevated lactate points towards an unmeasured osmotically active substance such as a toxic alcohol. Serum ketones help exclude diabetic or alcoholic ketoacidosis, salicylate and ethanol levels help exclude or identify those specific ingestions, and serum albumin is needed to correctly interpret the anion gap, since hypoalbuminaemia lowers the expected baseline anion gap and can mask a toxic ingestion if not corrected for.

questions.question: A 56-year-old man was found unconscious with a severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (pH 7.05–7.1, HCO3- 10 mEq/L), a history of alcohol use, and no pill bottles found; 3 empty beer bottles were nearby. He was intubated for airway protection. Blood ketone, alcohol, salicylate and paracetamol levels were negative; albumin was 3.8 mmol/L. He required high-dose noradrenaline and produced only 30 ml of urine over 2 hours; urinalysis showed multiple crystals. Based on this picture, ethylene glycol poisoning was diagnosed. Appropriate treatment for this patient includes:
questions.explanation: Traditional treatment of ethylene glycol poisoning consists of sodium bicarbonate, ethanol and haemodialysis. Fomepizole is a newer agent that inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing formation of the acidic, toxic ethylene glycol metabolites responsible for the anion-gap acidosis and renal injury; if patients are diagnosed and treated early, haemodialysis may sometimes be avoided, but once severe acidosis and renal failure have occurred — as here, with oliguria and crystalluria — haemodialysis is necessary. Activated charcoal does not bind ethylene glycol effectively and has no role.
